messages.content: I can't believe I actually got promoted at work after all the late nights and hard work! I'm absolutely thrilled—this validates my performance and I can't wait to raise the bar even higher and tackle bigger projects with even more energy.

messages.speaker: responder_agent
messages.content:
That is fantastic — huge congratulations! You earned it.

What’s the new title, and when do you start? What will change day-to-day (more people management, bigger projects, budget ownership)? I’d love to hear what part you’re most excited about and if anything feels a little daunting.

If you want, I can help with:
- a short announcement/email to your team or leadership,
- a 30/60/90-day plan to hit the ground running,
- ideas for an achievable “early win” to build credibility.

Quick tips to get started: prioritize the few things that will move the needle, schedule 1:1s with key stakeholders, delegate where possible, and set clear expectations with your team. How do you want to celebrate?

messages.speaker: persona_agent
messages.content: It's been a long journey—I've been working towards this for almost six months, and it feels surreal; I start as Senior Product Manager next Monday! I'm over the moon to own bigger projects and lead a small team (a bit nervous about people management), so yes please—help me draft a short announcement and a 30/60/90 plan, and I’ll celebrate with a fancy dinner!

messages.speaker: responder_agent
messages.content:
Congrats again — this is huge, and starting Monday is exciting! Below are a ready-to-send announcement plus a practical 30/60/90 plan and a few people-management tips and early-win ideas you can use right away. I can tailor anything here to your org or draft a LinkedIn post or Slack message if you want.

1) Short announcement (email or internal message)
Subject: Excited to step into the Senior Product Manager role

Hi team — I’m excited to share that I’ve accepted the Senior Product Manager role and will start next Monday. I’m grateful to everyone who’s supported me along the way, and I’m looking forward to partnering more closely with you to drive [product/area name] forward.

In this role I’ll be owning [high-level scope — e.g., “the onboarding and payments experience” or “the B2B integrations roadmap”], leading a small team, and focusing on prioritization, delivery, and customer outcomes. Over the next few weeks I’ll be scheduling 1:1s with stakeholders and the team to align on priorities and how I can best support your work.

Please reach out if you have immediate questions or if you’d like to catch up — I’m excited to get started!

Thanks,
[Your name]

Optional short Slack blurb:
Thrilled to share I’m stepping into the Senior Product Manager role starting Monday 🎉 I’ll be focusing on [scope]. I’ll set up 1:1s with folks soon — happy to chat anytime.

2) 30/60/90-day plan (practical, measurable)

30 days — Learn & stabilize
- Objectives: Build trust, understand product, customers, metrics, and immediate risks.
- Actions:
  - Schedule recurring 1:1s with each direct report and key stakeholders (PMs, Eng. leads, Design, Sales, CS, Data).
  - Review roadmap, active projects, OKRs, backlog, KPIs (activation, retention, revenue, etc.).
  - Run a “listening tour”: 30–45 minute chats with each stakeholder + a customer-facing session or customer support shadow.
  - Identify top 3 risks/blocks and one quick fix that will unblock the team.
- Deliverables:
  - One-page summary of product health, top 3 priorities, and proposed near-term focus.
  - Quick win implemented or plan to implement.
- Success metric: Stakeholder alignment validated, 1:1s scheduled, quick win executed or scoped.

60 days — Align & deliver
- Objectives: Align team and stakeholders on priorities; deliver an early tangible outcome.
- Actions:
  - Facilitate a roadmap/strategy session to set or refine next quarter’s priorities and trade-offs.
  - Launch a focused experiment or deliver an incremental release that improves a key metric.
  - Start coaching/directing your team on execution and problem solving; assign clear owners and timelines.
  - Create/update team-level success metrics (OKRs or KPIs).
- Deliverables:
  - Short roadmap with committed deliverables and owners.
  - One experiment or feature released with tracked impact.
- Success metric: Delivery of the committed incremental release / experiment and initial data showing impact.

90 days — Scale & set strategy
- Objectives: Demonstrate impact, set longer-term strategy, and establish repeatable processes.
- Actions:
  - Analyze results from the 60-day release; iterate or scale if successful.
  - Propose a 6–12 month product strategy/vision aligned to company goals.
  - Implement regular cadences (planning, retrospectives, cross-functional syncs).
  - Begin development plans for direct reports (career conversations, goals).
- Deliverables:
  - 6–12 month product roadmap draft.
  - Team operating rhythm + 1–2 process improvements (e.g., improved prioritization framework).
- Success metric: Clear performance improvement in target KPIs and team cadence established.

3) People-management starter kit (for your first weeks)
- First 1:1 agenda (30–45 min): quick personal check-in (2–3 min), wins & blockers, priorities this week, career/development interest, feedback for me. End with actions & follow-ups.
- Frequency: weekly or biweekly 1:1s at first; increase frequency for direct reports who need more support.
- Quick rapport questions: What’s your preferred working style? What would success look like for you this quarter? Any immediate blockers I should know about?
- Feedback approach: praise publicly, coach privately. Give early praise quickly; address recurring issues with private, specific examples + suggested change.
- Growth plans: have a short development conversation by 60 days (aspirations, learning needs, stretch projects).

4) Early-win ideas
- Fix a high-friction UX bug or onboarding step that repeatedly causes drop-off — quick measurable impact.
- Prioritize and ship a small experiment that targets a leading metric (activation or retention).
- Reduce a cross-team blocker by negotiating a small trade or resource reallocation.
- Deliver a concise metrics dashboard or single-page product health report that stakeholders love.

5) Quick templates & tips
- Your first week: set up 1:1s, get access to dashboards, read recent postmortems, shadow support/customer calls.
- Communicate clarity: after your listening tour, send a 1-page memo with top insights and your near-term priorities — people appreciate clarity.

Phase 0: immediate prep (before day 1)
- Gather basics: role description, current OKRs/KPIs, org chart, active projects list, pending decisions, and key metrics dashboard access.
- Schedule these recurring meetings now: weekly team meeting, weekly leadership update, 1:1s with direct reports and your manager (biweekly if overloaded), and 30–60–90 review checkpoints.

Days 1–30: Learn fast, build rapport, deliver 1–2 quick wins
Goals:
- Build credibility and rapport.
- Clarify expectations and success metrics.
- Deliver at least 1 clear, visible quick win.

Actions:
- Stakeholder mapping and intro meetings (30–45 minutes each):
  - Clarify their priorities, pain points, expectations of you, preferred communication style, and success metrics.
  - Ask: “What would success look like for us in 90 days?” and “What should I avoid?”
- Team kickoff (first week):

  - Run a short team workshop to surface top obstacles and ideas for quick wins.
- Quick wins (choose 1–2 from these examples):
  - Fix a recurring process bottleneck (e.g., reduce meeting cadence, standardize a report).
  - Deliver/close a small project that’s already near completion.
  - Resolve a long-standing stakeholder gripe by implementing a simple change.
  - Publish a short “how we’ll work” doc that clarifies roles and communications.
- Delegation triage:
  - Audit your current tasks and those of the team. Use three buckets: keep, delegate, stop/postpone.
  - For each direct report, identify 1–2 tasks they can own now and one stretch opportunity.
- Early metrics:
  - Define 3–5 success metrics for the 90-day window (e.g., delivery milestones, stakeholder satisfaction, cycle time reduction).

Deliverables by day 30:
- 30-day summary for your manager: insights, confirmed priorities, proposed 60-day plan.
- 1 documented quick win and its impact.
- Delegation plan draft (who owns what, transition timeline).

Days 31–60: Execute, embed changes, expand delegation
Goals:
- Execute larger initiatives.
- Deepen stakeholder alignment.
- Transfer operational work so you can focus on strategy.

Actions:
- Run a “priorities review” session with stakeholders to confirm roadmap adjustments.
- Start delegating with structure:
  - Create clear outcome statements for each delegated task (what success looks like, constraints, dependencies, timeline).
  - Set check-in cadence: short weekly syncs + shared status doc or dashboard.
  - Provide training or pairing sessions for new owners.
- Mid-sized wins to aim for:
  - Implement a process change (e.g., a new intake workflow or SLA).
  - Deliver a first milestone of a larger project demonstrating momentum.
- Update metrics and report progress to manager and stakeholders.

Delegation mechanics (practical steps):
- Use the “S.T.A.R.” method when delegating:
  - Situation: context and why this matters.
  - Task: the specific output expected.
  - Authority: decisions they can make.
  - Reporting: how and when to update you.
- Agree on boundaries and escalation paths up front.
- Document procedures as you go (short playbooks) — this reduces repeated questions and makes future delegation smoother.
- Reward/recognize early wins by direct reports publicly to reinforce ownership.

Deliverables by day 60:
- 60-day review: progress vs. metrics, delegation state, updated 90-day priorities.
- At least one process/operational responsibility transitioned to a direct report.
- A playbook or runbook for repeated tasks.

Days 61–90: Scale impact and set longer-term strategy
Goals:
- Consolidate gains and shift focus to strategic priorities.
- Institutionalize delegation and reporting.
- Prepare a 6–12 month plan.

Actions:
- Conduct a team retrospective on changes made and refine processes.
- Measure outcomes of quick wins and process changes; communicate results organization-wide if impactful.
- Finalize long-term priorities with your manager and stakeholders, including resource needs and risks.
- Delegate higher-level operational ownership (budget, vendor ops, hiring decisions) as appropriate.
- Coach direct reports for career growth and capability building to sustain momentum.

Deliverables by day 90:
- 90-day report: wins, measurable impact, stakeholder feedback, lessons learned, and proposed 6–12 month roadmap.
- Fully documented delegation model (roles, SLAs, escalation).
- Development plans for each direct report aligned to upcoming priorities.

  - How we should work together & communication preferences (10)
  - Immediate asks for first 90 days & success indicators (10)
  - Next steps & follow-ups (5)
- Delegation script (30–60 seconds when handing over):

- Quick-win selection criteria:
  - High visibility / low complexity
  - Fast time-to-impact (<30 days)
  - Low cross-org dependencies
  - Demonstrable metric improvement (or clear stakeholder relief)

Success metrics examples
- Project delivery: % of milestones met on time
- Process efficiency: cycle time reduction, meeting hours saved
- Stakeholder satisfaction: Net Promoter Score or simple 1–5 rating after interactions
- Team growth: number of responsibilities successfully transitioned; direct reports’ confidence level

Common pitfalls & how to avoid them
- Holding on to tasks: Force yourself to delegate 20–30% of current work in month 1 and increase over time.
- Vague delegation: Always define outcomes, authority, and reporting.
- Skipping stakeholder conversations: Prioritize the top 10 relationships and meet them early.
- Not measuring impact: Pick 3 metrics early and review weekly.

30–60–90 Plan (Senior Product Manager)
Purpose: balance strategy + execution while establishing leadership with former peers.

High-level objectives
- 30 days: Learn, align, and get early credibility (listen, clarify, quick wins).
- 60 days: Execute and embed operating rhythms (deliver initial initiatives, delegate more).
- 90 days: Drive strategy and scale (present a cohesive plan, show measurable progress).

Success metrics (examples — pick ones relevant to your org)

- Delivery: % of committed milestones hit in next quarter.
- Team engagement: 1:1 feedback scores (baseline → improvement).
- Customer impact: a leading product metric (activation, retention, NPS) moves X%.

30 days — Listen, clarify, quick wins
- Meet 1:1 with every direct report (30–60 min) to understand priorities, blockers, career goals.
- Meet key stakeholders: engineering lead, design lead, sales, support, data, and your manager. Clarify expectations, success criteria, and timelines.
- Create a stakeholder map + decision RACI.
- Audit current roadmap and metrics; identify one or two obvious quick wins you can unblock in 30 days.
- Establish your operating cadence: weekly PM/eng sync, monthly product review, 1:1 schedule.
- Deliverable: summary document for manager/stakeholders with top priorities, quick wins, and proposed cadence.

60 days — Align, delegate, deliver
- Finalize and communicate a prioritized 90-day roadmap aligned to business outcomes.
- Start executing quick wins; track progress publicly in the team channel or dashboard.
- Implement a delegation/decision framework: ownership for each feature, escalation path, and definition of “decision by you vs. by the team.”
- Run a product discovery/research session to validate assumptions for bigger bets.
- Coach and enable former peers: set clear role boundaries and expectations in recurring 1:1s; identify one direct report to mentor for leadership growth.
- Deliverable: updated roadmap, progress report on quick wins, and a clear RACI for upcoming features.

90 days — Scale strategy, measure impact
- Present a cohesive product plan to leadership: outcomes, roadmap, resourcing needs, and success metrics.
- Measure and share early results from initiatives (impact vs. baseline).
- Build talent/skill plan: gaps, hiring or training needs, and development plans for your team.
- Institutionalize rituals: product reviews, post-mortems, planning sessions.
- Deliverable: leadership presentation + team retrospective with next-quarter objectives.

Managing former peers — practical language & actions
- One-on-one script starter: “I value our working relationship and the work you do. In this new role I’ll be responsible for prioritization and strategy — I want your candid input and I’ll be transparent about decisions. How can I support you best during this transition?”
- Set clear role definitions publicly (org doc) to remove ambiguity.
- Delegate visible ownership to them quickly — trust + accountability builds credibility faster than telling.
- Be consistent and fair when making decisions; explain rationale rather than just issuing orders.
- Handle pushback privately: acknowledge input, explain constraints, and invite trial/experiments when feasible.

I’m grateful for the support that got us here and I’m committed to focusing our work on the customer outcomes and priorities that move the business forward. 3) Cohort & query templates
Assumptions: events table named events(user_id, account_id, event_name, event_time TIMESTAMP, properties JSON), users table named users(user_id, account_id, created_at TIMESTAMP).

A) Activation rate within 30 days (Postgres / standard SQL)
-- activation = workflow_run
WITH signups AS (
  SELECT user_id, created_at AS signup_time
  FROM users
  WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2026-03-01' AND '2026-03-31'
),
activated AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT s.user_id
  FROM signups s
  JOIN events e ON e.user_id = s.user_id
  WHERE e.event_name = 'workflow_run'
    AND e.event_time BETWEEN s.signup_time AND s.signup_time + INTERVAL '30 days'
)
SELECT
  (COUNT(DISTINCT activated.user_id)::decimal / COUNT(DISTINCT signups.user_id)) AS activation_rate
FROM signups
LEFT JOIN activated ON activated.user_id = signups.user_id;

B) Activation rate within 30 days (BigQuery SQL syntax)
-- BigQuery TIMESTAMP_ADD
WITH signups AS (
  SELECT user_id, created_at AS signup_time
  FROM `project.dataset.users`
  WHERE created_at BETWEEN TIMESTAMP('2026-03-01') AND TIMESTAMP('2026-03-31')
),
activated AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT s.user_id
  FROM signups s
  JOIN `project.dataset.events` e
    ON e.user_id = s.user_id
  WHERE e.event_name = 'workflow_run'
    AND e.event_time BETWEEN s.signup_time AND TIMESTAMP_ADD(s.signup_time, INTERVAL 30 DAY)
)
SELECT
  SAFE_DIVIDE(COUNT(DISTINCT activated.user_id), COUNT(DISTINCT signups.user_id)) AS activation_rate
FROM signups
LEFT JOIN activated ON activated.user_id = signups.user_id;

C) Weekly retention cohorts (users active in week N after signup week)
-- return rate per cohort week for weeks 0..12 (Postgres-like)
WITH signups AS (
  SELECT user_id, date_trunc('week', created_at) AS cohort_week
  FROM users
  WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-03-31'
),
activity AS (
  SELECT user_id, date_trunc('week', event_time) AS activity_week
  FROM events
  WHERE event_time >= '2026-01-01'
)
SELECT
  s.cohort_week,
  a.activity_week,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN a.activity_week = s.cohort_week THEN a.user_id END) AS week0_active,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN a.activity_week = s.cohort_week + INTERVAL '1 week' THEN a.user_id END) AS week1_active,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN a.activity_week = s.cohort_week + INTERVAL '2 week' THEN a.user_id END) AS week2_active
FROM signups s
LEFT JOIN activity a ON a.user_id = s.user_id
GROUP BY s.cohort_week, a.activity_week
ORDER BY s.cohort_week;

(Recommend building a pivot in your BI tool for visualization; can adapt to your environment.)

30/60/90-Day Plan (high-level objectives, actions, and deliverables)

30 days — Learn, build trust, and map the landscape (Listen & Diagnose)
- Objectives
  - Establish relationships with your six direct reports and key cross-functional partners (Engineering, Design, Sales, CS, Marketing, Ops).
  - Understand product strategy, current roadmap, KPIs, tech health, delivery cadence, and major customer pain points.
  - Identify immediate risks and 1–2 quick wins.
- Actions
  - Hold 1:1s with each direct report (first 10–14 days). Run stakeholder 1:1s with leads in Eng, Design, PMM, Sales, CS.
  - Read core docs: roadmap, PRDs, OKRs, recent post-mortems/retros, user research, analytics dashboards, backlog, release notes.
  - Sit in sprint planning, standups, and a retrospective. Shadow support/sales calls or review recent customer escalations.
  - Run a product teardown: top flows, funnel metrics, customer feedback themes, and tech debt hotspots.
  - Request and review metrics: MAU/DAU, retention, activation, conversion funnels, MRR/ARR (if applicable), NPS/CSAT, bug counts, cycle time.
- Deliverables (end of 30 days)
  - 1-page “30-day findings” memo: key strengths, top 3 opportunities, top 3 risks, recommended immediate actions/quick wins.
  - Documented stakeholder map with communication cadence.

60 days — Align around priorities and start delivering early wins (Design & Iterate)
- Objectives
  - Align the team and stakeholders on short-term roadmap priorities and success metrics.
  - Implement 1–2 quick wins and improve delivery processes where they block outcomes.
  - Clarify roles, responsibilities, and decision rights on the team.
- Actions
  - Run a roadmap review workshop: reprioritize based on impact/effort, dependencies, and business goals.
  - Introduce any immediate process fixes: clearer sprint planning, definition-of-done, backlog grooming cadence, or release checklist.
  - Pilot an instrumentation/analytics improvement (if metrics gaps exist) to measure feature impact.
  - Start regular cross-functional planning syncs (weekly or biweekly).
- Deliverables (end of 60 days)
  - Updated roadmap v0.1 with clear outcomes & metrics (RACI/decision log).
  - 6–12 week delivery plan with milestones and owners.
  - Evidence of 1–2 early wins (reduced cycle time, resolved high-impact bug, adoption bump, etc.).

90 days — Execute, scale, and demonstrate measurable impact (Drive & Measure)
- Objectives
  - Show measurable outcomes from implemented changes and the roadmap.
  - Cement the team’s delivery cadence and operating model.
  - Surface longer-term strategy and resourcing needs.
- Actions
  - Execute major items from the 6–12 week plan and measure results against KPIs.
  - Host a 90-day review with leadership and stakeholders summarizing outcomes, learnings, and next roadmap.
  - Identify hiring or reorganization needs, and propose growth plans for your reports.
  - Create a repeatable reporting cadence and a playbook for how your team works cross-functionally.
- Deliverables (end of 90 days)
  - 90-day outcomes report (metrics vs targets, launched features and impact, process improvements).
  - Roadmap & resourcing plan for the next 6–12 months.
  - Individual development plans for each direct report or proposals for promotions/hiring as needed.

Suggested success metrics to track
- Delivery: sprint predictability (planned vs delivered), cycle time, number of hotfixes.
- Product impact: feature adoption, activation rate, conversion lift, retention, MRR/ARR impact.
- Quality/customer: bug escape rate, CSAT/NPS, number of escalations.
- Team health: 1:1 satisfaction, churn/intention to stay, velocity stability.

Practical quick-win ideas
- Fix the highest-severity recurring bug or unblock a stalled customer issue.
- Clarify a confusing KPI and add it to the weekly dashboard.
- Remove a small process overhead (e.g., excessive approvals) that speeds delivery.
- Run a small experiment with a target metric (conversion lift, onboarding tweak).

One-on-one structure + questions

Cadence & logistics
- Frequency: weekly or every other week (30–45 minutes). Prefer weekly for the first 60 days to build rapport.
- Pre-meeting ask (send the day before): “Top 3 items to discuss + any blockers (1–2 slides/screenshots).”
- Agenda template (30–40 min)
  1. Quick personal check-in (2–3 min)
  2. Wins & progress since last meeting (5–8 min)
  3. Current priorities and blockers (10–15 min)
  4. Career development & feedback (8–10 min, alternate focus weekly)
  5. Action items and commitments (2–3 min)

First 1:1 (build trust + gather context)
- Tell me about your background and proudest accomplishments on this product/team.
- What are your current responsibilities and top priorities?
- What part of your work energizes you, and what drains you?
- What are the biggest blockers or frustrations you face day to day?
- Are there customers or accounts you’re particularly close to? Any recent customer stories I should know?
- How do you prefer to receive feedback? How do you like to be recognized?
- What are your 6–12 month career goals?
- If you could change one thing immediately about the product or team process, what would it be?
- What do you need from me in the next 30 days to be successful?

Follow-up / Execution-focused 1:1 (ongoing)
- What are the most important things you’re working on this week and why?
- Where are you blocked? Who do you need me to unblock or escalate to?
- What assumptions are we making about users/metrics, and how can we test them quickly?
- Which stakeholders need alignment or communication this week?
- Any tech or quality concerns we should surface now?
- Any feedback for me on priorities, communication, or support?

Career & growth 1:1 (monthly/quarterly)
- What progress have you made toward your 6–12 month goals?
- What skills/experiences do you want to develop next? What opportunities would help?
- What stretch project would excite you?
- How can I help you prepare for the next role/promotion?
- Any feedback on team structure, hiring, or role clarity?

Questions to learn product & customers quickly (good for early 1:1s)
- Who are our top 5 customer segments and the biggest pain for each?
- Which 3 metrics best represent product health for our business?
- What recent decisions are we most unsure about, and why?
- Which experiments or features have surprised you (positive or negative) in the last 6 months?
- Who are our product’s strongest advocates and strongest critics inside the company?

Tips for running these 1:1s effectively
- Start with listening: spend majority of first meetings asking and noting.
- Take action quickly on small asks — it builds trust.
- Keep a running doc of each direct report’s goals, risks, and career plan.
- Alternate focus: one week execution, next week development/feedback.
- Give public recognition for wins and protect heads-down time for deep work.

1) Tailored 30/60/90-day plan for a Senior PM at a B2B SaaS scale-up (~200 people), measured on activation, retention, and ARR (starts May 15, team of six)
- Overarching focus: shorten time-to-value for new customers (activation), reduce churn and increase expansion (retention & ARR), and tighten delivery/measurement to prove impact.

30 days — Listen, map, and baseline
- Objectives
  - Build relationships and trust with your six reports and key partners (Eng, Design, CS, Sales/AM, RevOps, PMM).
  - Baseline the metrics that matter: activation funnel, first 30/90-day retention cohorts, churn reasons, expansion/upsell velocity, and ARR movements.
  - Identify 1–2 immediate, high-impact quick wins that move activation or retention.
- Actions
  - 1:1s with each direct report + product-adjacent leads (CS managers, sales leads, PMM, analytics owner, engineering manager).
  - Pull top dashboards and raw cohort analyses (activation funnels, time-to-first-value, NPS/CSAT by cohort, renewal rates, expansion ARR).
  - Review top customer segments, onboarding flows, pricing/packaging docs, and recent win/loss and churn post-mortems.
  - Sit in a CS/AM call and a sales demo to hear onboarding and buyer pain first-hand.
- Deliverables (end of 30 days)
  - 30-day findings memo (one-page summary — see template below) with: top 3 opportunities (activation/retention/ARR), top 3 risks, recommended immediate actions (quick wins), and measurement gaps to fix.

60 days — Align priorities, ship quick wins, and improve measurement
- Objectives
  - Align stakeholders on a prioritized short-term roadmap that targets activation lift and churn reduction.
  - Ship 1–2 quick wins and establish better instrumentation for meaningful metrics.
  - Clarify decision rights for prioritization between growth/CS/eng.
- Actions
  - Run a cross-functional roadmap workshop to prioritize by ARR impact and customer lifetime value.
  - Implement measurement fixes: events/metrics for onboarding milestones, cohort tracking, and revenue attribution for expansions.
  - Deliver quick wins (examples below): onboarding flow tweak, targeted in-product prompts, a churn-prone flow fix, or a renewal/expansion playbook.
  - Start weekly cross-functional sync with CS & Sales to escalate at-risk accounts and surface product blockers.
- Deliverables (end of 60 days)
  - v0.1 Roadmap with outcomes and north-star metrics (activation %, 30/90-day retention, expansion ARR target).
  - Evidence of early impact (A/B or before/after cohort change, reduced onboarding time, identified top 10 at-risk accounts mitigated).

90 days — Drive measurable ARR/retention improvements and scale operations
- Objectives
  - Demonstrate measurable improvements in activation/retention/ARR from shipped initiatives.
  - Cement operating model for ongoing product–CS–Sales collaboration and forecasting for ARR impact.
  - Present resourcing plan for next 6–12 months (hiring, tooling, analytics).
- Actions
  - Execute on mid-term roadmap items (automation of onboarding, expansion triggers, pricing/packaging tests).
  - Host a 90-day review with leadership including data-backed results and recommended investments (e.g., more CS headcount, analytics engineer, automation).
  - Create playbooks for handoffs (sales → onboarding → CS) and product support for strategic accounts.
- Deliverables (end of 90 days)
  - 90-day outcomes report: KPIs vs targets, feature list and measured impact, customer stories, recommended investments.
  - Roadmap and resourcing plan tied to projected ARR lift and retention improvements.
  - Individual development plans for direct reports.

Quick-win ideas specifically for B2B SaaS
- Reduce time-to-first-value: remove or streamline the longest onboarding step; ship an in-product guided checklist.
- Target high-churn cohort: run a focused outreach + product tweak for that cohort; measure 30-day retention lift.
- Expansion trigger emails/in-product CTA for accounts with usage signals (seat growth, power-user activity).
- Renewal risk dashboard: top 20 at-risk accounts with recommended actions and an SLA for outreach.
- Fix one recurring enterprise integration/bug blocking pilot customers.

A) Team (direct reports + immediate stakeholders)
Subject: Excited to join as Senior Product Manager — quick intro + 1:1s
Hi team — I’m excited to join as Senior Product Manager, officially starting May 15. I’ll be leading the product roadmap and delivery for [product area], and I’m looking forward to partnering closely with each of you.

My immediate priorities in the first month are: listening and learning, baselining activation/retention/ARR metrics, and identifying a couple of quick wins to unblock value for customers. I’ll be booking 1:1s with each of you over my first two weeks to understand your work, blockers, and how I can help.

Please feel free to send anything you think would help me prepare (top 3 priorities, current blockers, key docs, and any customer stories). Looking forward to meeting you and to what we’ll build together.

30–60–90 day plan (Senior Product Manager)

Goals and structure
- 30 days — Learn & assess: build context, relationships, and a baseline.
- 60 days — Align & plan: synthesize findings, set priorities, and start delivering.
- 90 days — Execute & scale: measure impact, improve processes, and expand influence.

30 days — Learn & assess (Goals: understand product, users, metrics, and people)
- Meet 1:1 with manager, direct reports (if any), product team, engineering leads, design, data, sales, CS, marketing, and key stakeholders.
- Audit metrics/KPIs (DAU/MAU, retention, conversion, NPS, revenue, activation, funnel leaks).
- Review roadmap, backlog, major initiatives, and outstanding technical or UX debt.
- Read customer feedback, support tickets, user research, and recent release post-mortems.
- Map stakeholders and decision rights; identify influencers and blockers.
- Deliverables: stakeholder map, product health summary (top 5 metrics), list of quick wins and immediate risks, and an initial 30-day reflection note shared with your manager.

60 days — Align & plan (Goals: get consensus on priorities and start shipping)
- Run discovery sessions for top opportunities; validate with quantitative and qualitative data.
- Create prioritized roadmap/initiative list (with clear outcomes and metrics).
- Start 1–2 quick-win experiments or feature improvements to demonstrate impact.
- Establish or optimize team rituals (planning cadence, triage, retrospective format).
- Define success metrics and instrumentation needs; partner with data/analytics to create dashboards.
- Begin mentoring/coaching product peers and clarifying expectations for cross-functional partners.
- Deliverables: 60-day roadmap with success criteria, experiment plans, initial dashboards, and a stakeholder alignment memo.

90 days — Execute & scale (Goals: show measurable impact and embed process improvements)
- Ship and measure outcomes from the experiments/quick wins started in month 2.
- Refine roadmap based on results; propose OKRs or roadmap for the next quarter.
- Improve or formalize product discovery process and handoff to engineering.
- Drive cross-functional alignment on at least one major initiative (roadmap commitment).
- Identify hiring or resource gaps and propose a plan.
- Deliverables: results report (metrics from releases), updated roadmap/OKRs, process playbook or templates, and a 90-day presentation to leadership.

Success metrics and risks
- Example success metrics: feature adoption percentage, lift in conversion/activation, reduction in time-to-ship, improved NPS, team confidence and alignment scores.
- Common risks: unclear priorities, incomplete instrumentation, stakeholder misalignment. Mitigations: early alignment meetings, clear success criteria, weekly check-ins, and visible dashboards.

Communication cadence
- Weekly 1:1 with your manager, biweekly cross-functional syncs, monthly stakeholder updates, public roadmap/metrics dashboard.

Promotion announcement / thank-you notes

Internal announcement (company or team email)

I look forward to continuing our collaboration — please reach out if you have feedback or ideas you’d like to discuss.

Thanks again for the support — I’m energized to get started!
[Your name]

LinkedIn announcement (short)

Thank you so much for your support and for trusting me with the Senior Product Manager role. I deeply appreciate the mentorship and opportunities you’ve given me — especially [specific example]. I’m committed to delivering measurable outcomes in this role and supporting the team as we scale. I’d love to schedule a 30-minute sync to align on expectations and priorities for my first 90 days.
Thanks again,
[Your name]

Thank-you note to your team
Hi team,
I’m excited to share that I’ve been promoted to Senior Product Manager. I couldn’t have done this without your partnership, late-night problem-solving, and candid feedback. I’m committed to making our processes smoother, delivering outcomes that matter to customers, and supporting each of you however you need. Let’s build great things together!
— [Your name]

Quick tips for announcing
- If sending company-wide, copy your manager and mention concrete focus areas so people know what to expect.
- For LinkedIn, keep it upbeat and brief; thank mentors and teammates and link to your company.
- Personalize thank-you notes with a specific example or moment to make it meaningful.

messages.content:
Amazing—congrats again. Below is a practical, ready-to-use 30/60/90-day plan tailored to a Senior Product Manager for a payments platform, plus two high-impact “quick wins” you can realistically deliver in the first 30–60 days. I’ll keep it actionable so you can copy/paste or adapt straight away.

High-level summary
- 30 days (Discover & Stabilize): get up to speed, baseline metrics, quick triage of most urgent failures, pick quick wins. Deliver: a findings doc + prioritized backlog and selected quick-win plan.
- 60 days (Deliver & Iterate): implement quick wins, instrument monitoring, run experiments, show measurable improvement. Deliver: KPIs improved, dashboards, MVPs.
- 90 days (Scale & Strategy): roll out durable fixes, embed processes, present roadmap and goals to execs. Deliver: final impact report, product roadmap, and operating SLAs.

30-day plan — objectives, actions, deliverables
Objectives
- Learn the system and stakeholders fast.
- Establish baseline metrics and the biggest sources of payment failure/latency/cost.
- Identify and start 1–2 quick wins.

Key actions (week-by-week)
- Week 1: Stakeholder onboarding
  - 1:1s: engineering lead, payments ops, fraud, risk/compliance, finance, customer support, sales/merchant success, SRE.
  - Read: architecture docs, runbooks, incident postmortems, existing roadmaps, SLAs, top customer complaints.
  - Set up access: dashboards, logs, analytics, alerting tools.
- Week 2: Baseline metrics & data dive
  - Pull KPIs: authorization success rate, decline breakdown (by reason/gateway), chargeback rate, settlement latency, reconciliation exception rate, MTTR for incidents, conversion funnel impact.
  - Map payment flows and third-party integrations (gateway providers, acquirers, processor failover).
- Week 3: Customer & ops insights
  - Shadow payments ops and customer support for a day each.
  - Interview 4–6 top merchants/customers about payment pain points.
  - Identify the top 3 sources of payment loss/cost.
- Week 4: Prioritize & plan
  - Deliverable: 30-day findings doc with top issues, root causes, and a prioritized backlog (impact vs effort).
  - Choose 1–2 quick wins and create an implementation plan (owners, milestones, KPIs).
  - Schedule 30/60/90 review with manager and stakeholders.

Success metrics for 30 days
- Baseline dashboard created and shared.
- Top 3 pain areas identified and a prioritized backlog created.
- Quick-win plan selected and resourced.

60-day plan — objectives, actions, deliverables
Objectives
- Execute quick wins and begin measurable improvements.
- Improve observability and incident response.
- Validate hypothesis with experiments/metrics.

Key actions
- Implement quick-win #1 and #2 (see suggestions below) with clear owners and daily standups for the first 2 weeks of work.
- Build or enhance a payments health dashboard (real-time authorization rate, decline reasons, gateway latency, reconciliation exceptions).
- Add alerts for key thresholds (e.g., sudden drop in auth rate, spike in chargebacks, settle lag).
- Run A/B tests or canary rollouts for UX or retry logic changes.
- Continue stakeholder 1:1s and bi-weekly syncs with engineering and ops.

Deliverables
- Working quick-win implementations with initial results.
- Monitoring & alerting in place.
- Updated roadmap + resource plan for the next quarter.

Success metrics for 60 days
- Quantified improvement on quick-win KPIs (e.g., +X% authorization rate, Y% fewer manual reconciliations).
- Reduced MTTR or time to detect incidents by a measurable factor.
- Roadmap and resourcing aligned with execs.

90-day plan — objectives, actions, deliverables
Objectives
- Turn early wins into durable product/operational changes.
- Set strategic product priorities for the payments platform.
- Institutionalize ownership, runbooks, and SLAs.

Key actions
- Harden fixes: edge cases, performance testing, cross-region failover.
- Document and publish runbooks and SLA expectations.
- Integrate payment metrics into product OKRs and report cadence.
- Present 90-day review to leadership with data-backed recommendations for next 6–12 months (e.g., processor consolidation, fraud tooling, new payment methods).
- Propose org/process changes (new hires, rotations, on-call adjustments).

Deliverables
- Final impact report (before/after metrics).
- 6–12 month roadmap and OKRs.
- Runbooks and monitoring playbooks handed to operations.

Success metrics for 90 days
- Permanent reduction in key pain metric(s).
- Clear product roadmap approved with resource commitments.
- Stakeholder satisfaction and adoption of runbooks.

Two high-impact quick wins (choose 1–2)

Quick win A — Reduce auth declines from top N reasons (high ROI)
Why: Authorization declines are the most direct revenue leak. Fixing a few high-frequency reasons often yields immediate gains.
Steps (2–4 weeks)
1. Analyze decline data: top 5 decline codes by volume and by revenue impact (card network codes, issuer codes, gateway errors).
2. For each major category define treatment:
   - UX messaging for soft declines (e.g., “try another card” with inline guidance).
   - Automated retry rules (e.g., retry certain transient network errors with backoff).
   - Route to alternative acquirer/gateway for specific failure signatures.
   - Improve card-on-file expiration detection and pre-emptive communication.
3. Implement config changes and small front-end UX tweak or server-side retry logic.
4. Monitor auth-rate and conversion funnel for uplift. Roll back if negative customer impact.
Owners: Payments engineering, UX, payments ops, analytics.
KPIs to watch: auth success rate, payment conversion rate, failed attempts per session, revenue recovered.
Risk & mitigation: Improper retries could double-charges — use idempotency, test with small cohorts.

Quick win B — Payments health dashboard + alerting (quick visibility, low friction)
Why: Faster detection = faster resolution. Many issues are due to lack of real-time visibility.
Steps (1–3 weeks)
1. Define critical metrics and thresholds (auth rate, gateway latency/errors, settlement lag, reconciliation exceptions).
2. Build a dashboard (Grafana/Looker/BigQuery, etc.) and add real-time alerting to Slack/pager.
3. Create a one-page incident playbook for each alert type: owner, runbook link, initial remediation steps.
4. Run a fire-drill to validate MTTR improvement.
Owners: SRE, payments engineering, analytics, ops.
KPIs to watch: time-to-detect, time-to-resolve, # of incidents/week.
Risk & mitigation: Avoid alert fatigue — tune thresholds, add a suppression window for known noisy signals.

Suggested prioritization: If you must pick only one to start, do the dashboard + alerting first (Quick win B) — it helps detect and measure the issues you’ll try to fix in Quick win A.

Practical templates (copy/paste)

- Intro message to stakeholders (1–2 sentences): “Hi all—new Senior PM for Payments. Over the next 30 days I’ll be running a rapid audit to baseline metrics and propose 1–2 quick wins. I’ll share findings on [date]. Please point me to any docs/owners I should meet.”

Meeting agendas (first 1:1 with engineering lead)

- 10 mins: current blockers or active incidents.
- 10 mins: expectations, communication cadence, escalation paths.

- Or I can tailor the plan to your org if you tell me: gateway/processor stack, current top KPIs, and whether you have analytics access.

Quick asks:
- Please point me to any docs/runbooks/dashboards that are essential (links are great).
- If you’re the owner of payments tooling, ops, fraud, finance, or merchant success, could we schedule a 20–30 min sync in the next 7 days? I’ll send calendar invites.
- I also need read access to: [analytics platform], [logs], [dashboards], [alerting system]. If you can grant or direct me to the correct approver, that helps.

Priority contacts I’d like to meet early:
- Engineering lead: [name]
- Payments ops: [name]
- Fraud/Risk: [name]

If I missed someone who should be in this loop, please add them or let me know who to contact. Looking forward — excited to get started.

C. Step‑by‑step checklist — Quick Win A: Reduce auth declines (practical, ~2–4 weeks)
Goal: Recover revenue by addressing the top 3–5 decline reasons (technical + UX + routing). Target metric: +X% auth success for affected flows within 30–60 days.

Phase 0 — Prep (Day 0–2)
- Confirm owners: Analytics, Payments Eng, UX, Ops. Assign a single PM owner (you).
- Create a short Slack channel or project board for the work.
- Ensure access to raw auth logs, payment gateway logs, and dashboarding tools.

Phase 1 — Data & diagnosis (Day 1–5)
- Query/aggregate declines by:
  - decline_code (card network/issuer/gateway)
  - gateway/processor
  - merchant/product
  - time-of-day / geography / device type
- Output: table with decline_code, count, revenue impact estimate, top gateways, top merchants.
- Identify top 3–5 decline codes by revenue impact and frequency.
- For each decline code, classify as: permanent (card declined/insufficient funds), transient (timeout/network), fraud/blocked, or configuration (misrouting, currency mismatch).

Phase 2 — Define treatments (Day 3–7)
For each high-impact decline_code, pick one or more treatments:
- UX messaging: custom inline message for soft declines (e.g., “try another card” + suggested next steps).
- Automated retry rules: only for transient network/gateway timeouts; define backoff strategy (e.g., retry 1 time after 2–5s).
- Route to alternative gateway/acquirer: for patterns showing gateway-specific failures.
- Pre-emptive checks: card-on-file expiry detection, BIN routing for known issuer quirks.
- Manual ops play: temporary merchant outreach or manual capture for high-value transactions.

Document: treatment plan per decline code with owner, estimated dev effort, success metric, and risk.

Phase 3 — Safety & design (Day 5–9)
- Safety checks:
  - Ensure idempotency keys are enforced before retries to prevent double-charges.
  - Only retry if initial response indicates no final settlement (e.g., network timeout or gateway 5xx).
  - Set retry cap (1 retry recommended initially) and only for validated error codes.
- UX: draft short messages and confirm with legal/comms if needed (no misleading language).
- Approvals: sign-off from engineering lead and payments ops for routing changes and retries.

Phase 4 — Implementation (Day 7–14)
- Break into small tasks and implement behind a feature flag:
  - Server-side retry logic with idempotency and backoff (Payments Eng).
  - Gateway routing rule(s) update (if applicable) in configuration, not hard code.
  - UX message changes (Frontend/UX).
  - Analytics events to mark retried flows and final outcome.
- Create automated tests and unit tests for new logic; smoke tests for routing.

Phase 5 — Canary & rollout (Day 10–17)
- Canary rollout:
  - Start with 1–5% of traffic or a single low-risk merchant/region.
  - Monitor: auth success rate for the cohort, conversion funnel, duplicate charge incidence, error logs.
- Monitoring queries/alerts to watch:
  - auth_success_rate_by_cohort
  - number_of_retries / retry_success_rate
  - duplicate_charge_count (if tracked)
  - chargeback rate delta (longer term)
- Thresholds to stop rollout (example):
  - Any increase in duplicate_charge_count > 0 for canary → pause and investigate.
  - Significant drop in conversion in cohort (e.g., > 2 standard deviations) → roll back.

Phase 6 — Measure & iterate (Day 14–21)
- Compare pre/post metrics for the affected decline codes:
  - auth success rate delta
  - conversion funnel lift
  - revenue recovered estimate
  - ops tickets related to payments
- Validate there’s no rise in duplicates or chargebacks. If there is, stop and revert.
- If results positive, increase rollout to 25% then to 100% in controlled increments.

Phase 7 — Operationalize & document (Day 18–30)
- Add permanent dashboards and alerts for the treated decline codes and retry metrics.
- Update runbooks with the new retry behavior, routing rules, and UX messaging.
- Hand off to payments ops with clear owner and SLAs.
- Communicate results to stakeholders: quick summary with before/after numbers and next priorities.

Risks & mitigations (short list)
- Duplicate charges: enforce idempotency, only retry on non-final error codes.
- Increased chargebacks: monitor chargeback rate closely for several weeks after rollout.
- Alert noise: tune alerts and aggregate retry metrics separately.
- Merchant impact: run canaries with lower-risk merchants first; coordinate with merchant success.

Acceptance criteria (what “done” looks like)
- Implementation deployed behind feature flag and progressively rolled out.
- Measured increase in auth success rate for targeted decline codes (target = +X% — set your goal).
- No meaningful increase in duplicate charges or chargebacks.
- Runbook & dashboard updated and owners assigned.

Quick templates to use internally

- Short status update to execs (1–2 lines):
  - “Implemented targeted retry + UX for top decline codes. Canary results: +Y% auth success for cohort; no duplicates observed. Rolling to 25% next.”

- Draft the exact SQL/Looker queries to pull the decline breakdown if you tell me your analytics platform (BigQuery / Redshift / Snowflake / etc.).
- Draft the small UX copy examples and the feature-flag rollout plan.

3) A/B test plan for UX copy variants (canary rollout)
Goal: determine which UX copy reduces abandonment during payment declines and/or increases completed payments when automatic retry is in play.

Hypotheses:
- H0: UX copy variations produce no difference in completed-payment conversion in the decline cohort.
- H1: UX copy variant B (e.g., “We’re retrying automatically”) increases conversion for users who encounter targeted decline codes versus Variant A/C.

Experiment design
- Population: users who encounter a targeted decline code (one of the decline codes you are treating) during checkout.
- Randomization: assign users (or sessions) randomly to variant A, B, C at the moment the decline event occurs. Persist assignment for the session. Prefer user-level randomization if a user may see the message multiple times.
- Variants:
  - A: Concise — “Payment failed due to a temporary error. We’re retrying — no action needed.”
  - B: Actionable — “Payment couldn’t be completed. Try another card or wait — we’re retrying automatically.”
  - C: Fallback/permanent — “We couldn’t process this card. Please try a different payment method or contact your bank.”
- Primary metric: conversion rate = fraction of decline-cohort sessions that ultimately complete a successful authorized payment within X minutes (e.g., 10 minutes) after the decline event.
- Secondary metrics: retry_success_rate (fraction of retried attempts that become authorized), time_to_success (median seconds), duplicate_charge_count, chargeback_rate (longer-term: 30d), user-initiated retry actions (e.g., clicked “try again”).
- Safety metrics / stop signals: any non-zero duplicate_charge_count in the cohort, or a statistically significant increase in chargebacks (monitor after rollout).

Sample size guidance (quick approximate)
- For a baseline conversion rate p0 (e.g., 10% of declined sessions convert after retry) and a minimum detectable uplift delta (absolute, e.g., +2 percentage points = 0.02), sample size per group (two-sided, alpha=0.05, power=0.8) roughly:
  n ≈ 2 * (Z_{1-α/2} * sqrt(p0*(1-p0)) + Z_{power} * sqrt(p1*(1-p1)))^2 / (p1 - p0)^2
  where p1 = p0 + delta, Z_{1-α/2} = 1.96, Z_{power}=0.84
- Example: p0=0.10, delta=0.02 => p1=0.12 yields n ≈ ~15k per variant. (This is a rough estimate — smaller deltas need large samples.)
- If you can only canary on a small % of traffic, run for longer until sample targets are met.

Duration
- Run until minimum sample per variant is reached OR at least 7–14 days of business cycles (to capture weekday/weekend patterns) — whichever is longer.

Assignment & instrumentation
- Create an experiment assignment table or store variant in transactions/events:
  - experiment_name STRING
  - experiment_variant STRING
  - user_id STRING (or session_id)
  - assigned_at TIMESTAMP
- Track events:
  - decline_shown (with decline_code, variant)
  - retry_attempted (true/false, retry_count)
  - payment_authorized (transaction_id, amount, gateway)
  - duplicate_charge_flag (if detected)
  - chargeback_event (later)
- Ensure analytics events include experiment_variant to query results.

- Compute counts & conversion rate per variant (BigQuery):
-- replace EXPERIMENT_NAME and assignment table / transaction table names
WITH declines AS (
  SELECT
    e.user_id,
    e.experiment_variant,
    e.decline_code,

    e.experiment_name = 'decline_copy_canary'
    AND DATE(e.assigned_at) BETWEEN DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 30 DAY) AND CURRENT_DATE()
),
outcomes AS (
  SELECT
    d.experiment_variant,
    COUNT(DISTINCT d.user_id) AS users_exposed,
    SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM `PROJECT.DATASET.TRANSACTIONS_TABLE` t
      WHERE t.user_id = d.user_id
        AND LOWER(t.status) = 'authorized'
        AND t.event_time BETWEEN d.decline_time AND TIMESTAMP_ADD(d.decline_time, INTERVAL 10 MINUTE)
    ) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS converted_within_10m
  FROM
    declines d
  GROUP BY d.experiment_variant
)
SELECT
  experiment_variant,
  users_exposed,
  converted_within_10m,
  ROUND(100 * SAFE_DIVIDE(converted_within_10m, users_exposed), 3) AS conversion_pct
FROM outcomes
ORDER BY experiment_variant;

- Compute retry success rate and duplicate counts:
SELECT
  e.experiment_variant,
  COUNT(1) AS retried_attempts,
  SUM(CASE WHEN LOWER(t.status) = 'authorized' AND t.is_retry = TRUE THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS retry_successes,
  SUM(CASE WHEN t.duplicate_flag = TRUE THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS duplicates_detected,
  ROUND(100 * SAFE_DIVIDE(SUM(CASE WHEN LOWER(t.status) = 'authorized' AND t.is_retry = TRUE THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), COUNT(1)), 2) AS retry_success_rate_pct
FROM
  `PROJECT.DATASET.TRANSACTIONS_TABLE` t
JOIN
  `PROJECT.DATASET.experiment_assignments` e
ON
  t.user_id = e.user_id
WHERE
  e.experiment_name = 'decline_copy_canary'
  AND DATE(t.event_time) BETWEEN DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 30 DAY) AND CURRENT_DATE()
GROUP BY e.experiment_variant;

Statistical test (quick approach)
- Use counts from the first query (converted_within_10m and users_exposed per variant).
- Compute z-test for proportions in Python (example):

Python snippet (run locally / in notebook):
import math
from mpmath import erfc  # or use scipy.stats if available

# sample numbers from BigQuery output
n1 = 15000      # users_exposed for variant A
x1 = 1500       # converted_within_10m for variant A
n2 = 15000      # users_exposed for variant B
x2 = 1650       # converted_within_10m for variant B

p1 = x1 / n1
p2 = x2 / n2
p_pool = (x1 + x2) / (n1 + n2)
z = (p1 - p2) / math.sqrt(p_pool * (1 - p_pool) * (1/n1 + 1/n2))

# two-sided p-value using normal CDF via math.erfc
p_value = 0.5 * math.erfc(-z / math.sqrt(2))

print("p1", p1, "p2", p2, "z", z, "p-value", p_value)

Notes:
- If you have scipy available, use scipy.stats.proportions_ztest for convenience.
- If p-value < 0.05 (two-sided) and effect is in the predicted direction, you can consider variant beneficial.

Stopping / rollout rules
- Stop immediately if:
  - Any duplicate_charge_count > 0 in canary cohort (unless explainable).
  - Chargeback rate increases materially for the cohort.
- Continue to roll out only if safety metrics are stable and primary metric improves or neutral.
- Ramp plan: 1% → 5% → 25% → 100% traffic, each step with at least 24–48 hours of monitoring and minimum sample thresholds.

- If winner, implement UX variant as default and remove experiment flag. Update runbooks and dashboards.

  - Institutionalize healthy processes and a cadence for product strategy & delivery.
- Key activities
  - Launch or scale major initiatives from the 60-day plan.
  - Establish regular product reviews with execs (monthly OKR reviews, quarterly roadmap review).
  - Formalize 1:1 development plans and promotion/career paths.

  - Roadmap for next 6–12 months with clear KPIs and dependencies.
  - Team org adjustments or hiring plan (if needed).
- Success metrics
  - Demonstrated impact on at least 2 product metrics or business KPIs.
  - Improved delivery predictability (sprint velocity stability, on-time releases).
  - Positive feedback from direct reports and key stakeholders.

Practical tips & quick wins
- First two weeks: prioritize relationship-building—people are more open when they feel heard.
- Focus on one measurable quick win (small release, customer fix, process change).
- Use data to drive prioritization; if data’s thin, plan a rapid research spike.
- Keep communication frequent and transparent—weekly updates and a short monthly wins email.

messages.content:
Huge congrats — I love how much this means to you. Below is a tailored 30/60/90 plan for a ~6-person SaaS product team focused on reducing churn and tackling a large backlog, plus two announcement versions (short Slack and slightly longer email to the team/execs). If you want, I can plug in concrete KPI targets once you share current churn/backlog numbers and your exact start date.

30 days — Listen, learn, stabilize (find the biggest churn drivers & triage backlog)
- Objectives
  - Understand why customers are leaving (qualitative + quantitative) and establish a repeatable backlog triage process.
  - Build trust with the ~6-person team and align on immediate priorities.
- Key activities
  - 1:1s (60 min) with each team member + short role/responsibility map (who owns what now).
  - Quick data audit: MRR, monthly churn (gross & net), cohort retention (7/30/90d), trial conversion, activation funnel, feature usage, NPS/CSAT, payment failure rate.
  - Run a cancellation/exit-flow review (look at cancellation reasons and any automated win-back flows).
  - Backlog triage session: label items (bug/tech debt/feature/customer-request), size quick/medium/large, and tag by expected churn impact.
  - Sit in team rituals (planning, demo, retro) and observe process bottlenecks.
- Deliverables
  - One-page “State of the Product” with top churn hypotheses, backlog snapshot (estimated points or count by category), and immediate risks.
  - Backlog triage output: prioritized list of top 10 items (with rationale: revenue/churn/effort).
  - Stakeholder map and immediate communication cadence (weekly syncs).
- Success metrics
  - Completed 1:1s with everyone.
  - Baselines for the key metrics listed above.
  - Backlog triaged and top 3–5 items agreed for short-term action.

60 days — Prioritize, run experiments, deliver quick wins
- Objectives
  - Deliver measurable reductions in near-term churn drivers and prove one or two backlog items yield value.
  - Improve predictability in delivery and reduce noise from urgent issues.
- Key activities
  - Launch 2–4 targeted experiments focused on highest-probability churn drivers (see experiments list below).
  - Create a lightweight prioritization framework (RICE or Impact/Effort + “churn impact” multiplier) and use it to build a 60–90 day roadmap.
  - Implement one process change to reduce context switching (e.g., dedicated bug day, WIP limits, or 20% capacity for incidents/tech debt).
  - Start pairing PM/engineer on at least one backlog item to speed delivery.
  - Deep-dive with customer success on top-churn segments and top support tickets.
- Deliverables
  - Prioritized 60–90 day roadmap with owners and success metrics.
  - At least one measurable quick win shipped (e.g., onboarding tweak, payment retry flow).
  - Experiment results baseline and go/no-go decisions.
- Success metrics
  - Experiment(s) show positive signal (e.g., improved activation or reduced cancellations in test cohort).
  - Team adoption of prioritized process and clearer sprint predictability.
  - Reduction in high-priority open bugs / backlog items (absolute or percent).

90 days — Execute, scale, institutionalize
- Objectives
  - Demonstrate measurable improvement in churn and begin to sustainably reduce backlog through process and hiring/skill adjustments.
  - Establish cadences for metrics reviews and product strategy.
- Key activities
  - Roll out or scale successful experiments (onboarding flows, pricing nudges, win-back campaigns).
  - Formalize monthly product & metrics review with execs and CS.
  - Build or update playbooks: cancellation handling, onboarding, release checklist, incident response.
  - Assess hiring or reallocation needs (e.g., more CS, SRE effort, or a growth PM).
  - Do a 90-day retrospective and publish learnings + next-quarter roadmap.
- Deliverables
  - 90-day impact report: experiments & releases vs metrics, backlog reduction, customer feedback insights.
  - Updated 6–12 month roadmap with KPIs and resource plan.
- Success metrics
  - Measurable drop in cohort churn (or improvement in retention curve) attributable to changes.
  - Reduced critical backlog items and improved delivery predictability.
  - Positive feedback from team and CS on product direction and collaboration.

Quick high-impact experiments & quick wins to prioritize (start with those that are low-effort / high-churn-impact)
- Onboarding: reduce time-to-value (shorten steps, add checklist, in-app guided tour, or welcome email flow).
- Cancellation flow & win-back: add a short exit survey, offer self-serve pause options, or an automated win-back email + trial extension.
- Payment recovery: retry logic and dunning emails to recover involuntary churn.
- Email/feature nudges: targeted engagement campaigns for at-risk cohorts (usage drop signals).
- First 7-day activation funnel optimization (A/B test flows or copy that drives activation).
- Triage “bug bash” or dedicate one sprint to top-priority bugs/technical debt that cause churn.
- CS + PM weekly sync for top at-risk accounts (hand-raise process).
- Quick pricing/packaging audit for obvious mismatches causing churn.

Backlog prioritization rubric (practical)
- For each item score: User impact (revenue/retention), Frequency (how many users affected), Effort (dev/design/test), Risk/Dependency.
- Add a “churn impact” multiplier for items directly linked to cancellations or support escalations.
- Use RICE or a 2x2 (impact vs effort) to separate “must-fix now” vs “defer.”

Key metrics to track (set baselines in week 1)
- Primary: Monthly churn rate (gross & net), cohort retention (D7/D30/D90), MRR churn, trial conversion rate, activation rate (time-to-first-value).
- Secondary: NPS/CSAT, support ticket volume by type, payment failure rate, feature usage for core flows.
- Operational: sprint predictability (planned vs delivered), mean time to resolve incidents, backlog size by priority.

Team & process suggestions for a ~6-person team
- Weekly 30-min product + CS sync to review top at-risk customers.
- Weekly backlog triage + grooming (keep to 30–45 min).
- Limit WIP: prioritize 2–3 sprint-level priorities and protect capacity for incidents/tech debt (~15–25%).
- Make owners explicit for churn-related work: one person owns win-back flows, one owns onboarding experiments, etc.

Announcement templates

1) Short Slack (friendly)

Over my first month I’ll be meeting with each of you 1:1 to learn what’s working, what’s blocking you, and where you see the biggest opportunities—especially around reducing churn and cleaning up our backlog. I’ll follow up with a short 90-day plan after those conversations. If there’s anything urgent you want me to know before then, DM me. Can’t wait to work with you all in this next chapter! —[Your name]

2) Short email to managers/execs (slightly longer)
Subject: My transition to Product Team Lead — priorities & next steps

My immediate focus will be two-fold: reduce churn and bring the backlog under control so we can focus on high-impact work. I’d welcome a 30-min sync with each of you in the first two weeks to align on expectations and dependencies. Thanks for the support — looking forward to driving measurable improvement together. —[Your name]

Next steps I can help with now

- Customize KPI targets and a 90-day dashboard if you share current metrics (churn %, MRR, backlog size, team roles).

Which of those would you like me to prepare next? Also, what’s your exact start date and can you share current churn and backlog baselines?

messages.content:
Love this—congrats again. Below are the two deliverables you asked for: a ready-to-run 1:1 question set with a simple agenda, and a copy-paste-friendly backlog triage template plus scoring rubric and runbook. I can drop these into a Google Sheet/CSV for you if you want — or customize further once you send the churn/backlog baselines.

1) 1:1 question set + agenda (60 minutes recommended)
Agenda (60 min)
- 5 min — Quick check-in (how are you doing?)
- 40 min — Core discussion (role, work, blockers, priorities)
- 10 min — Career/development + feedback to you
- 5 min — Commitments & next steps

Core questions (pick ~6–8; let them lead)
- Context & goals
  - What are you most proud of from the last 3 months?
  - What are your top goals for the next quarter?
  - Where do you want to have more impact in this role?
- Product & customers
  - Which product areas do you think are most responsible for churn right now?
  - What customer feedback or support themes worry you most?
  - Which features are getting the most/least usage? Any surprises?
- Backlog & execution
  - Which backlog items do you think must be prioritized now, and why?
  - What’s blocking you from delivering the work you think matters?
  - How often do urgent firefights pull you away from planned work?
- Process & collaboration
  - What’s working well between product, engineering, and CS? What’s not?
  - Are there meetings/processes we should stop, start, or change?
- Career & development
  - Where would you like to grow this year? What support do you need?
  - Are there stretch projects you want ownership of?
- Feedback to you (the new lead)
  - How can I best support you in the next 30/60/90 days?
  - Anything I should avoid doing/doing differently as I step in?

Close
- Confirm 1–2 concrete actions for them and for you.
- Agree on a follow-up (time/date) and any data/notes they should prepare for the next check-in.

Quick tips
- Send the agenda + 2–3 pre-reads (current priorities, backlog snapshot) 24–48 hours before each 1:1.
- Keep a running notes doc per person with commitments, wins, and career goals.
- For junior/ICs, lean heavier on career/dev questions; for senior PM/engineer, emphasize scope/strategy and blockers.

2) Backlog triage template + scoring rubric (copy into spreadsheet)
Columns (use these as spreadsheet columns)
- ID
- Title
- Type (bug / tech debt / feature / experiment / support request)
- Short description
- Reporter / Requester (customer, sales, CS, internal)
- Affected users (estimate or segment)
- Frequency (1–5; 1=rare, 5=very common)
- Reach (1–5; how many users affected)
- Impact (1–5; user/business impact if unresolved)
- Revenue impact (1–5; direct/indirect MRR effect)
- Customer escalations (count)
- Churn impact (0/1/2; 0 = no link, 1 = potential contributor, 2 = direct cause of cancellations)
- Effort (T-shirt or story points; use numeric e.g., 1, 3, 8, 13)
- Dependencies (other teams / blockers)
- Suggested action (Now / Next / Backlog / Blocked)
- Owner
- Target delivery / ETA
- Notes / Links (tickets, recordings)
- Date logged

Scoring rubric & formula
- Use 1–5 scales for Frequency, Reach, Impact, Revenue impact.
- Churn impact is a small integer multiplier (0/1/2) to give heavier weight to items linked to cancellations.
- Priority Score (example formula you can use in a sheet):
  PriorityScore = (Impact*3 + Reach*2 + Frequency*2 + RevenueImpact*3 + CustomerEscalations*2 + ChurnImpact*5) / Effort
- Interpretation (example thresholds):
  - PriorityScore > 6: Now / High
  - 3–6: Next / Medium
  - <3: Backlog / Low
Adjust weights if you want more/less sensitivity to churn or revenue.

Sample row (illustrative)
- ID: B-102
- Title: Checkout failure on renewals
- Type: bug
- Reporter: CS (top 10 accounts)
- Frequency: 4
- Reach: 3
- Impact: 5
- Revenue impact: 5
- Customer escalations: 8
- Churn impact: 2
- Effort: 3
- Suggested action: Now
- Owner: Eng-A
- Target delivery: 2 weeks
- Notes: Payment gateway timeout; see ticket #453

Runbook: how to run a 45–60 min triage session (weekly or biweekly)
- Prework (owner)
  - Populate rows for all candidate items before the meeting.
  - Tag items that need discussion (high score change or new).
- Attendees
  - Product lead (you), engineering lead, CS lead, one PM/engineer, optionally sales/ops for revenue-impact items.
- Meeting flow (45 min)
  - 5 min — Quick state: backlog counts & top metrics
  - 25–30 min — Review top ~8 items by current PriorityScore; confirm scores, dependencies, and decide action
  - 10 min — Reassign owners & target ETAs; agree on 1–2 unblock items for immediate attention
  - 5 min — Document decisions, update the sheet, and communicate to stakeholders
- Outputs
  - Updated backlog spreadsheet with action column set
  - Owners and ETAs for all “Now” items
  - Quick broadcast to CS/sales if anything affects customers/accounts

Final notes & next steps
- I can:
  - Convert this into a Google Sheet with formulas and a dashboard.
  - Create a one-page 1:1 template (note-taking format) you can duplicate for each report.
  - Customize scoring weights once you send current churn % and backlog counts (you said you’ll send baselines by EOD).
- Want me to create the Google Sheet now and share a link, or would you prefer a downloadable CSV? Also, do you want a short scheduler message I can draft to book the 1:1s for the first two weeks of June?

Great — I’ll prepare everything so you can hit the ground running. Quick note: I can’t directly create a Google Sheet in your Drive from here, but I’ll give you a ready-to-paste template (headers + formulas), a dashboard recipe, and a downloadable CSV option if you want. If you prefer I actually create the Sheet for you, you can either share an editable Drive link or invite a placeholder account (we can coordinate how). Otherwise, copy/paste the content below into a new Google Sheet and the formulas will work.

1) Backlog / triage sheet — headers (paste into row 1 of a sheet named "Backlog")
A: ID
B: Title
C: Type
D: Short description
E: Reporter
F: AffectedUsers
G: Frequency (1–5)
H: Reach (1–5)
I: Impact (1–5)
J: RevenueImpact (1–5)
K: CustomerEscalations (numeric)
L: ChurnImpact (0/1/2)
M: Effort (story points or numeric)
N: Dependencies
O: SuggestedAction
P: Owner
Q: TargetDelivery
R: Notes/Links
S: DateLogged
T: PriorityScore (computed)

2) PriorityScore formula (paste into T2 and drag down)
=(I2*3 + H2*2 + G2*2 + J2*3 + K2*2 + L2*5) / M2

3) Auto-set SuggestedAction (optional) — put this in O2 and drag down (overrides manual editing)
=IF(T2>6,"Now",IF(T2>=3,"Next","Backlog"))

4) Conditional formatting suggestions (Backlog sheet)
- PriorityScore (column T)
  - >6 → fill red (high)
  - 3–6 → fill yellow (medium)
  - <3 → fill green (low)
- SuggestedAction (O)
  - "Now" → red, "Next" → orange, "Backlog" → green
Set these under Format → Conditional formatting.

5) Useful quick formulas for the Dashboard sheet
Create a new sheet named "Dashboard" and add these cells:

- Total items:
=COUNTA(Backlog!A:A)-1

- Count Now / Next / Backlog:
=COUNTIF(Backlog!O:O,"Now")
=COUNTIF(Backlog!O:O,"Next")
=COUNTIF(Backlog!O:O,"Backlog")

- Avg PriorityScore (ignoring blanks):
=AVERAGEIF(Backlog!T:T,">0")

- Sum effort for Now:
=SUMIF(Backlog!O:O,"Now",Backlog!M:M)

- Top 5 by PriorityScore (three-column view: ID, Title, PriorityScore):
=QUERY(Backlog!A2:T,"select A,B,T order by T desc limit 5",0)

6) Suggested charts for the Dashboard
- Pie chart: SuggestedAction distribution (Now/Next/Backlog)
- Bar chart: Top 5 PriorityScore (use the query result)
- Line chart (over time): backlog size by DateLogged — requires you to periodically append snapshots (see "Runbook" below)

7) Runbook / cadence (how to use the Sheet)
- Pre-meeting: owners add candidate items to Backlog sheet before triage.
- Weekly/biweekly triage (45–60 min):
  - Run Dashboard totals, review top 8–10 items by PriorityScore.
  - Confirm SuggestedAction, assign Owner and TargetDelivery.
  - Update Status (you may add a "Status" column: Open / In Progress / Blocked / Done).
- Keep a weekly snapshot row in a separate sheet "BacklogHistory" for trends (date, total open, total Now, avg priority).

8) Extra helpful columns you may add over time
- Status (Open/In Progress/Done)
- Sprint (if you track by sprint)
- CustomerImpactNote (link to ticket/customer record)

9) Export / CSV
If you want, I can generate a CSV file content for the Backlog header row and a couple of sample rows you can paste into a CSV and import. Tell me if you want that and whether you prefer sample rows filled with placeholders.

10) Next step I’ll do after you send baselines

- I can build a polished Google Sheet with the Dashboard and conditional formatting and share an editable file link — you’ll just need to give a sharing link or invite an email address I’ll provide.

11) Scheduler message to book your 1:1s (pick/send as Slack DM or email)
Short Slack DM (60 min default — adjust to 30 if you prefer):

Please pick a time that works for you here: [Your calendar link] (or reply with 2–3 times that work and I’ll book). Agenda: quick check-in, top priorities/risks, backlog items you think are critical, and how I can best support you. Looking forward to it — thanks!

If you prefer an all-team scheduling message to send once (so everyone picks slots from your calendar):

Over the first two weeks I’d like to meet 1:1 with each of you for ~60 minutes to learn about your priorities, blockers, and ideas for reducing churn and clearing the backlog. Please book a time on my calendar here: [Your calendar link] (slots available June 1–12). If none of those work, DM me with two alternatives and I’ll find a time. I’ll send a short agenda in the invite — feel free to add anything you want me to prepare. Thanks — excited to meet with you!

—[Your name]

If you want me to generate an invite text that includes the 1:1 agenda and a small pre-read checklist (what to prepare), I can add that to the calendar invite body.

---

Which do you want next?
- I can produce a downloadable CSV with header + 3 sample rows now.
- I can paste the full sheet-ready formulas (including the Dashboard with cell references) if you’d like the exact layout.
- Or, if you want me to create the actual Google Sheet and share it, tell me how you’d like to invite me (share link or guest email) and I’ll prepare it and return a shareable link.

Below are a ready-to-use 30/60/90 plan you can copy and adapt, plus two short announcement email options (friendly and formal). If you want, tell me your team size, top priorities, or any sensitivities and I’ll customize further.

30/60/90-day plan (template)
Purpose: Move from listening to defining priorities to delivering measurable impact while building trust and clarity.

First 30 days — Learn, listen, and stabilize
- Objectives
  - Build relationships and credibility.
  - Understand current priorities, pain points, and metrics.
  - Identify 1–2 quick wins.
- Actions
  - Meet your manager to align on expectations, authority, and success metrics.
  - Schedule 30–45 min 1:1s with each direct report (complete within 2–3 weeks).
  - Meet key stakeholders (peers, product, sales, support, engineering, customers if relevant).
  - Review key docs: strategy, roadmap, KPIs, org chart, active projects, recent retrospectives.
  - Run or observe team rituals (standups, planning, retro).
  - Deliver a quick win (e.g., resolve a blocking issue, clarify a process, remove a small bottleneck).
- Metrics / signals
  - 100% of core 1:1s completed.
  - List of top 5 pain points + proposed next steps.
  - One quick win completed and communicated.
- Risks to avoid
  - Making big changes before listening. Overcommitting your time.

Days 31–60 — Diagnose, align, and start to act
- Objectives
  - Validate priorities and propose initial changes.
  - Start delegating and empowering leads.
  - Launch 1–2 initiatives to improve delivery or team health.
- Actions
  - Share a short “what I heard” summary with manager and key stakeholders; invite feedback.
  - Host a team meeting to share your initial perspective and priorities (high-level).
  - Implement improvements targeting top pain points (process tweaks, role clarity).
  - Define 2–3 measurable goals for the next quarter (team OKRs or KPIs).
  - Hold recurring 1:1s and set team cadence (weekly syncs, monthly reviews).
- Metrics / signals
  - Clear, agreed-upon priorities and 2–3 team goals.
  - Improved predictability on one delivery metric (e.g., reduced blockers, improved sprint completion).
  - Direct reports feel heard and have clear owners for tasks.
- Risks to avoid
  - Micromanaging or moving too fast on structural changes.

Days 61–90 — Deliver, refine, and scale
- Objectives
  - Start delivering on the defined goals and institutionalize improvements.
  - Build long-term roadmap and talent/development plan.
- Actions
  - Launch the longer-term initiatives (roadmap, process, cross-team projects).
  - Finalize role/responsibility matrix and delegation plan.
  - Identify coaching/development needs and create growth plans for direct reports.
  - Review resourcing and escalate hiring or reallocation needs.
  - Present a 90-day summary + next-quarter plan to your manager and team.
- Metrics / signals
  - Progress on the top team goals (e.g., X% improvement in cycle time, Y% reduction in high-severity incidents, stakeholder satisfaction).
  - Clear ownership across initiatives and fewer ad-hoc escalations.
  - Visible momentum and team alignment on priorities.
- Risks to avoid
  - Letting recurring issues reappear; not following up on commitments.

Practical items to include everywhere
- 1:1 agenda template: wins/updates (5 min), priorities/roadblocks (10 min), career/growth (10 min), feedback/advice (5 min).
- Communication plan: weekly status email or short team sync, monthly metrics review, quarterly roadmap review.
- Quick-win ideas: streamline meeting cadence, reduce blockers in release pipeline, clarify definition of done, add a stakeholder weekly update.

Two announcement emails

Option A — Friendly, warm (short)
Subject: I’m excited to share — stepping into Senior Manager
Hi team —
I’m excited to share that I’ve accepted the Senior Manager role and will start next Monday. I’m really grateful for the support and collaboration that got us here — thank you.

My first priority is listening and learning. Over the next few weeks I’ll be scheduling 1:1s with everyone and meeting our key partners so I can understand what’s working and where we can improve. I’ll share a short summary of what I hear and a few early priorities after that.

If you have anything urgent to raise, please ping me or book a quick 1:1. I’m looking forward to working even more closely with you and helping our team do its best work.
— [Your name]

Option B — Concise, formal
Subject: Announcement: New Senior Manager
Hi all,
I’m pleased to announce that I’ve been promoted to Senior Manager and will begin the role on Monday. Thank you to everyone who supported and collaborated with me — I appreciate it.

In the coming weeks I’ll be meeting with each of you to understand priorities and opportunities. My immediate focus will be listening, clarifying goals, and identifying a couple of early improvements to help our delivery and team health. I’ll follow up with the team on next steps and priorities.

  - Measurable process improvement (e.g., reduction in triage time).

- Key actions:
  - Deliver one major milestone or feature that maps to a top objective; run post-launch analysis.
  - Review and iterate on strategy based on metrics and user feedback.

Days 1–30 — Listen & assess

- Overload on key people → action: redistribute work, temporary hires/contractors if needed

2) Focused 30–60–90 plan (target: Senior PM ramp + 2 measurable early wins)

30 days — Learn, align, and baseline
- Meet: 1:1s with manager, direct reports, PM peers, engineering lead, design lead, data, ops, sales/CS (complete high-level intro 1:1s).
- Audit: Product KPIs (activation, retention, conversion, cycle time), roadmap, backlog, tech debt, current experiments.

- Success criteria: Complete 15–20 stakeholder 1:1s; have a baseline for target metrics; manager sign-off on top priority area.

60 days — Plan and pilot
- Select 1–2 early-win initiatives based on impact/effort.
  Example early wins:
   1) Increase new-user activation by 10% in 90 days through onboarding flow experiments (A/B test 2 variants; metric = activation rate).
   2) Reduce feature time-to-release by 20% in 60 days by streamlining PR/QA and introducing a release checklist (metric = average cycle time for priority tickets).
- Run sprint-length experiments or pilot MVPs; define success metrics, owners, and timeline.
- Start delegating backlog maintenance and ops tasks to free time for strategy.
- Deliverables: Experiment plans, prioritized roadmap update, cross-functional kickoff.
- Success criteria: Experiment(s) live; measurable early improvements in the selected KPI(s) or clear learnings; backlog ownership reassigned.

90 days — Execute, measure, and scale
